name: Lajkonik
description: The Lajkonik is the hobby-horse rider of Kraków, a bearded figure in pointed Tatar dress and Mongol robes who parades the Old Town each year on the first Thursday after Corpus Christi, playfully striking onlookers with his gilded wooden mace to bring them good luck. Legend traces the custom to 1287, when Vistula raftsmen of the Zwierzyniec district, called włóczkowie, are said to have surprised and overwhelmed a sleeping Tatar raiding party camped by the river, then ridden into the city dressed in the captives' robes to celebrate their victory. The earliest written notices of the procession date from the 1730s and 1750s, and the mayor still greets the Lajkonik at the Main Market Square with a ceremonial ransom of money and a toast drunk from a chalice. The key elements of its costume, from the cream-crested head to the golden mace, were designed in 1909 by Stanisław Wyspiański, and the figure remains one of the unofficial symbols of Kraków, reproduced on trams, shop signs and festival posters.
source: Ethnographic studies of Kraków folk festivals

name: Rogatywka
description: The rogatywka is a four-pointed peaked cap of Poland, distinguished by a square crown whose corners fold out over the rim, evolved from the konfederatka worn by the Confederates of Bar in 1768-1772. Under the Second Polish Republic it became the standard headgear of the Polish Army, worn in khaki and grey by infantry and in crimson by the mounted uhlans, and variants served Polish units through the Second World War and into the modern armed forces. The four corners are traditionally said to mark the four quarters of the world or the soldier's virtues, and the cap also became a piece of civil national dress, still worn with folk costume, on ceremonial occasions and by marching bands. Because of its insurrection and wartime associations the rogatywka carries a heavy symbolic charge as a badge of Polish independence, and modern reproductions are made by military tailors for parades, re-enactments and formal dress.
source: Histories of Polish military dress

name: Wycinanka
description: Wycinanka is the Polish folk art of paper cutting, practised above all by village women from the nineteenth century, who folded and snipped dyed paper with heavy sheep shears to make flat wall decorations. Regional schools differ sharply: the celebrated cutouts of Łowicz build up layers of brightly coloured paper into leafy bouquets, rosettes and birds, while Kurpie makers favour single-colour, symmetrical designs such as the jedynak, cut from one folded sheet in black, red or gold. The cutouts were pasted on the whitewashed beams and walls of rural cottages, hung around holy pictures and given as wedding gifts, borrowing their motifs freely from embroidery, tile painting and woven bands. Though few farmhouses now display them in the old way, wycinanki survive as an emblem of Polish folk identity, taught in workshops and collected in ethnographic museums such as those at Łowicz and Warsaw.
source: Studies of Polish folk paper-cutting

name: Kraków Szopka
description: The Kraków szopka is a Nativity crib built as a glittering model of the city itself, cramming Wawel Cathedral, St Mary's Basilica, castle towers, spires and arcades into a many-storeyed facade of cardboard, tin foil and painted paper around the central stable. The tradition took shape in the nineteenth century, when Kraków bricklayers and building workers made portable cribs to earn money at Christmas, and it gained its civic form after 1937, when the first official contest was held; makers known as krakowianie still compete every first Thursday of December on the Main Market Square beside the Adam Mickiewicz monument. The best szopki show great technical ambition, with moving figures, hidden candle-lit interiors and window scenes re-enacting nativity and patriotic tableaux. In 2018 UNESCO inscribed the szopka tradition on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and collections such as the one in the Historical Museum of the City of Kraków preserve competition winners going back decades.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Kraków ethnography

name: Pomlázka
description: The pomlázka is a braided whip of fresh willow twigs that Czech boys carry on Easter Monday, when they go from house to house lightly switching girls and women to wish them health, freshness and beauty, receiving painted eggs and coloured ribbons in return. The name comes from pomladit, 'to make young again', and the custom preserves an old spring-renewal rite of driving out winter and coaxing new life, in which the willow, one of the first trees to bud, was held to carry special power. Skilled makers plait eight, twelve or even more rods into a smooth handle, bind the tip with ribbon and often add a pair of dangling tassels, weaving the whip anew each spring. In Moravia the same whip is called the šibačka and in Slovakia the korbáč, and after the morning round the girls may pour water or perfume over the boys in the related Easter-Monday wetting custom.
source: Czech and Slovak ethnography of Easter customs

name: Czech Glass Christmas Ornaments
description: Czech glass Christmas ornaments are hand-blown and hand-painted baubles made in the glass towns of northern Bohemia, above all around Jablonec nad Nisou and the Krkonoše foothills, where the craft grew out of the region's bead and glass-button industry in the mid-nineteenth century. Workers blew thin globes from molten glass, silvered them from inside with a solution that gave the characteristic metallic glimmer, and then painted them by hand with snow, berries, flowers or fairy-tale figures before hanging them from the family fir tree. The delicate ornaments became a celebrated export, so prized that Bohemian and Moravian glassmakers supplied Christmas trees across Europe and America for more than a century. A few family workshops still fire the baubles by mouth today, and the region's museums display both the finished ornaments and the wooden and metal tools of the old glasshuts.
source: Histories of Bohemian glassmaking

name: Fujara
description: The fujara is a very long overtone flute of the Slovak shepherds, the central instrument of the Podpoľanie region, made from elder, maple or ash wood and reaching 160 to 200 centimetres in length, with a short side tube that carries the wind to the main bore. It has only three finger holes, yet a skilled player produces a low, humming bass and high, crying overtones by overblowing, and the traditional repertoire imitates the gurgle of springs, the wind and long pastoral calls. Shepherds played the fujara while tending flocks on the slopes of Poľana, and each maker decorated the instrument individually with burnt or carved ornament, so no two fujaras are alike. UNESCO proclaimed the fujara and its music a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008, and it is now heard both at folk festivals in Detva and in concert music.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnomusicology

name: Drotárstvo (Wire Craft)
description: Drotarstvo is the Slovak craft of working iron wire, born in the eighteenth century when travelling drotári from the hills of northern Slovakia walked across Europe mending cracked pottery, glass and pipes with fine wire bindings. What began as tinkering became an art: journeymen and masters built up latticework jugs, birdcages, vases and small household utensils entirely from wire, and the reinforced pots with their neat braided seams were admired as folk masterpieces. The craft was carried by emigrant drotári as far as Russia, the Balkans and America, and the region around Považie in particular produced dynasties of wiremen. In 2019 UNESCO inscribed drotarstvo on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and museums in Bratislava and Považská Bystrica preserve both the tools and the elaborate wirework that survives from the trade's heyday.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnography

name: Valaška
description: The valaška is the small axe of the Carpathian shepherds, a light iron head set on a long wooden haft that reaches the waist, serving at once as walking staff, digging tool and weapon. Slovak bača shepherds and hikers of the High Tatras carry the valaška through the mountains, and its handle is often ornamented with engraved patterns or metal mountings that mark the maker and the owner. Folk legend places the valaška in the hand of Juraj Jánošík, the eighteenth-century outlaw of the Tatra country who is said to have robbed the nobles and shared the booty with the poor, and the axe became an attribute of highland identity as much as the flute and the pipe. In the twentieth century the valaška was adopted as an emblem of Slovak mountaineering and folk life, and carved examples are kept as souvenirs and in ethnographic collections.
material: forged iron blade, carved wood handle
source: Slovak folklore and highland ethnography

name: Bogrács
description: The bogrács is the black cast-iron cauldron of Hungarian outdoor cooking, a three-legged pot suspended from a chain over an open fire, in which gulyás, pörkölt and fish stew are boiled and stirred with a long wooden spoon. The vessel dates from the world of the herdsmen of the Hungarian Plain, who cooked their one-pot meals over campfires, and the same pot is still the centrepiece of bográcsgulyás gatherings at weekends, feasts and village festivals. Its size and weight vary from small two-litre pots to great cauldrons for hundreds of eaters, and the cast iron is seasoned by use, giving the stew its characteristic smoky savour. Cooking in the bogrács is a slow, sociable ritual - the meat is seared, onion and paprika added, and the pot tended for hours - and for many Hungarians the cauldron over flame is the very image of hospitality and good eating.
source: Hungarian culinary and folk ethnography

name: Matyó Embroidery
description: Matyó embroidery is the flamboyant floral needlework of the Hungarian town of Mezőkövesd and its surrounding villages, where from about the 1860s women stitched huge roses, tulips and pansies in red, blue and green silk thread on white linen. The style covered festive women's costume, shirts, aprons, pillowcases, tablecloths and wall hangings, and the bold single blooms grew ever larger as the local Matyó identity took shape at the turn of the twentieth century. Unlike the fine satin stitch of other Hungarian regions, Matyó work used long, loose stitches that give the flowers a sculpted, three-dimensional look. The craft, passed from mother to daughter, was inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2012, and embroiderers, fashion designers and textile artists in Mezőkövesd continue to develop it.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Hungarian textile studies

name: Székely Kapu
description: The Székely kapu is the carved wooden gateway of the Hungarian Székely villages of Transylvania, an oak structure built in two parts: a large wagon gate for carts and hay and a smaller door beside it for people on foot. The finest examples, carved from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, are covered with tulips, the tree of life, suns, rosettes and heraldic devices, and often bear inscriptions such as 'Isten hozott' ('God brought you') or the name and year of the householders. Folk belief held that the large gate belonged to the living and the small gate to the dead, who were carried through it one last time on their way to the grave. Because each gate recorded the family, the land and the faith of its owners, the surviving Székely gates - the earliest dated remnant is from Mikháza in 1673 - are read as genealogies in wood.
source: Hungarian and Székely ethnography of folk architecture

name: Cifraszűr
description: The cifraszűr is the decorated shepherd's cloak of the Hungarian Great Plain, a knee-length mantle of white felt cut from a single piece, split down the middle so the wearer can slip it over the shoulders and pin it under the chin. Its name pairs szűr, the plain cloak of Hungarian herdsmen, with cifra, 'ornamented', and indeed the best cifraszűr covers the felt with black, red and green wool applique arranged in rosettes, tulips, fringes and braided borders. Herdsmen wore the szűr against sun and rain and slept in it on the puszta, and a richly worked cloak was a sign of skill, wealth and pride, passed down in the family or given as a groom's gift. By the twentieth century the cifraszűr had moved from pasture to festival dress and museum collections, remaining a striking emblem of Hungarian shepherd culture.
material: white wool felt, coloured wool thread
source: Hungarian folk costume studies

name: Crown of Saint Stephen
description: The Holy Crown of Hungary, identified with the crown of the first king Saint Stephen I (ruled 1000-1038), is a circlet of gold hung with enamelled plaques, pearls and gemstones, with a distinctive cross set at an angle on top. Scholars date the surviving bands and figures to the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and the crown as it exists today was almost certainly assembled from older parts for later coronations, so its precise age and original form are still debated. It was used to crown Hungarian kings from the Middle Ages down to Charles IV in 1916, the last Hungarian coronation, and legend held that no ruler who wore it could ever be overthrown. Hidden in chests, walled into castles and smuggled abroad over the centuries, the crown returned to Hungary from the United States in 1978 and has been displayed in the Hungarian Parliament building since 2000 as the supreme symbol of Hungarian statehood.
aliases: Crown of Saint Stephen of Hungary
source: Academic studies of the Hungarian coronation insignia

name: Martenitsa
description: The martenitsa is the Bulgarian talisman of March, a twisted length of red and white yarn, often finished with beads or a small tassel, exchanged on 1 March to wish health, strength and good fortune for the new year. The red stands for life and the blood, the white for purity and spring light, and the name honours Baba Marta, the capricious old woman of folk belief whose moods are said to govern the early-spring weather. The martenitsa is worn on the wrist, lapel or neck until the wearer sees a stork, a swallow or the first blossoming tree, then it is tied to a fruit tree so the tree will bear, or slipped under a stone for luck. The custom, shared across Bulgaria and its neighbours, was inscribed in 2017 on the UNESCO Representative List through a joint file on 1 March cultural practices, and whole streets of Bulgaria are strung with martenitsi every spring.
source: Bulgarian ethnography of spring customs and UNESCO files

name: Kukeri
description: The kukeri are the masked dancers of the Bulgarian winter, men dressed from head to foot in sheepskin and goat-hide, crowned with tall carved wooden masks and hung about the waist with heavy bronze and copper bells, who process through villages around New Year and before Lent. Their dance - a hopping, swaying, bell-shaking performance - is meant to drive out evil spirits, ill luck and sickness and to bring health, fertility and a good harvest in the season to come. Masks differ from region to region: Pernik favours towering feathered and horned figures, while the Rhodope makers carve flatter, beast-like faces, and each costume can weigh tens of kilograms. Since 1966 the International Festival of Masquerade Games Surva in Pernik has gathered hundreds of groups every January, and in 2015 UNESCO inscribed the Surova folk feast of the Pernik region on the Representative List.
material: sheepskin, carved wood, goat hair, bronze bells
source: Bulgarian ethnography of winter ritual customs

name: Gaida
description: The gaida is the Bulgarian bagpipe, an instrument built from a whole tanned goatskin that serves as the air bag, with a chanter pipe for the melody and a single long drone pipe that sounds a constant bass note. Its bright, cutting tone comes from a single beating reed in the chanter, and a skilled player holds the bag under the arm, fingers the chanter's holes and taps out rhythms as he squeezes. The gaida is the leading instrument of Bulgarian folk music, accompanying the horo line dances at weddings, village feasts and festivals, and in the Rodopi mountains it is traditionally played for the slow, meandering dance tunes of the region. Because shepherds were the first players, the gaida is bound up with the pastoral life, and it remains the national instrument of Bulgaria, heard from folk ensembles to wedding bands.
source: Bulgarian ethnomusicology

name: Mărțișor
description: Mărțișorul is the Romanian March talisman, a red-and-white twisted silk thread finished with a small charm, coin or bead, given on 1 March as a wish of health, love and good luck for the coming year. The name and the month both come from martie, March, and folk memory links the custom to the return of spring and to the capricious weather-woman Baba Dochia, whose shepherding stories echo the alternating mild and cold spells of early spring. Worn on the wrist or pinned to the chest for the whole month, the mărțișor is taken off at the end of March and tied to the branch of a fruit tree, believed to bring the tree good luck and fertility. The tradition is shared with the neighbouring lands that joined the joint UNESCO file of 2017, and Romanian jewellers now cast the charms in gold and silver alongside the older coins and shells.
material: red and white silk thread, metal charm or coin
source: Romanian ethnography of spring customs and UNESCO files

name: Troiță
description: Troița is the wayside cross of Romania, a hand-carved wooden cross sheltered under a little roof, erected at crossroads, springs, bridges and village edges to protect travellers and to honour the dead. In the wood-carving country of Maramureș the crosses are true monuments, their beams covered with vine scrolls, geometric rosettes, suns and sometimes the image of the Crucified, with inscriptions naming the dead and the year, and the oldest surviving examples go back to the eighteenth century. The cross is set up by families for a departed relative, at the place of a sudden death, or as a vow, and passers-by cross themselves before it, so the troița stands at the meeting of Christian devotion and the old belief that crossroads and water were liminal, dangerous places. New troițe are still carved and raised every year, making the wayside cross a living school of Romanian folk woodcarving.
source: Romanian ethnography of folk architecture and religion

name: Dacian Gold Bracelets
description: The Dacian gold bracelets are heavy spiral arm rings of the ancient kingdom of Dacia, hammered from Transylvanian alluvial gold in the mid-first century BC and worn as ornaments and marks of rank, possibly also deposited as votive offerings. The surviving pieces, each forged from a single ingot into five to seven coils that end in serpent or animal heads, weigh between roughly 680 grams and nearly 1.2 kilograms, a concentration of royal wealth unmatched in the Balkans. Around two dozen were looted from ritual pits near the sacred precinct of Sarmizegetusa Regia, the Dacian capital in the Orăștie Mountains, between 1999 and 2001 and smuggled abroad; an international police operation has since recovered at least thirteen, and others remain missing. The recovered bracelets are displayed in the Historical Treasury of the National History Museum of Romania in Bucharest as masterpieces of Dacian goldwork.
source: Archaeological studies of the Sarmizegetusa Regia treasure

name: Šajkača
description: The šajkača is the traditional Serbian cap, a rounded woollen cap with a raised crown whose four points fold into a characteristic V shape, made from a single piece of cloth and worn without a visor. Its name honours the šajkaši, the eighteenth-century Serbian river troops who crewed the šajka boats of the Danube and Sava under Habsburg command and who first wore the shape. From the nineteenth century the šajkača spread beyond the river garrisons to Serbian soldiers, teachers, priests and peasants, becoming a badge of Serbian national identity, worn in the Balkan Wars and the First World War and banned by the occupiers during the Second. The V of the crown is sometimes read as the spread wings of the eagle, and today the cap is worn at ceremonies, in folk ensembles and by diaspora Serbs as a mark of origin and belonging.
source: Histories of Serbian military dress and ethnography

name: Pirot Kilim
description: The Pirot kilim is a handwoven wool rug of the town of Pirot in southern Serbia, built on a vertical loom with a cotton warp and a dense woollen weft that produces a flat, reversible fabric. Weavers worked in the so-called vratilnice technique, knotting and braiding the weft in long strips so that the patterns interlock, and the classical designs pair a central medallion with borders of zigzags, hooks and stylised flowers in red, black, white and green. In the nineteenth century Pirot rugs hung on walls, covered floors and chests and formed part of the bride's dowry, and the town's weavers supplied households across the Balkans and the Ottoman court. Woven by women who guarded the pattern-books on the same looms, the Pirot kilim is counted a Serbian national symbol, and a small circle of masters still weaves it today.
source: Serbian textile and craft studies

name: Opanak
description: The opanak is the traditional leather shoe of the Serbian countryside, a soft moccasin cut from a single piece of cured pig or calf hide, stitched at the heel and gathered over the foot with thongs that cross above the ankle. Its most striking feature is the turned-up toe, the špic, which lifted the foot clear of dew, grass and stones and, in the most famous regional pattern, curls back into a small horn over the instep. Opanci were worn with woollen footcloths called obojci and tied with long straps, and they served peasants, herdsmen and even soldiers for centuries before factory footwear displaced them. Because almost every village had its own cut - the wide Šumadija form, the sharp Bosnian toe, the flat Montenegrin sole - the opanak became a strong marker of Serbian folk dress and is still worn at festivals, by folk dancers and on ceremonial occasions.
source: Serbian folk dress studies

name: Ohrid Pearl
description: Ohrid pearls are handmade jewellery pearls of North Macedonia, built up from a ground shell core coated with layer after layer of a milky emulsion made from the scales of the plasica, a small silvery fish endemic to Lake Ohrid. Because the recipe and the painstaking process are guarded as family secrets, only two families - the Talevs, who bought the formula in 1924, and the Filevs, who learned it in 1928 - have made authentic Ohrid pearls, passing the craft from father to son and hand-coating each grain up to ten times. Local tradition credits the secret to Jovan Subanović, a Russian emigrant said to have brought the technique to Ohrid after the 1917 revolution, and the name 'Ohrid Pearl' was fixed by 1935. Their soft lustre and durability made them famous beyond the Balkans; Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana are said to have worn them, and a handmade necklace remains a proud family heirloom.
source: Macedonian craft and jewellery studies

name: Dvojanka
description: The dvojanka is a double flute of North Macedonia, carved from a single piece of wood, sometimes elder or ash, as two parallel pipes joined at the mouth, with fingerholes on one pipe only. The second, unholed pipe serves as a drone, sounding a steady note beneath the melody and giving the instrument its haunting, reedy character; regional names include dvojnica, and similar double flutes are known across the Balkans. Shepherds played the dvojanka in the mountains, and it accompanied the slow, ornamented tunes of Macedonian pastoral music, the whistle of the drone carrying over pasture and dance ground alike. A small community of folk musicians and instrument makers keeps the dvojanka alive today, and it is heard at ethnographic concerts and village festivals alongside the kaval and the gaida.
source: Macedonian ethnomusicology

name: Chokha (Georgian Men's Coat)
description: The chokha is the traditional men's coat of the Caucasus, a long woollen garment with a fitted waist, a flared skirt and, most distinctively, rows of small cartridge cases - the gazyr - sewn diagonally across the chest. The gazyr began as real ammunition holders, with silver, wood or bone caps, and survived as ornament long after firearms made them obsolete, so the decorated chest became the emblem of Caucasian dress. In Georgia the chokha has been worn since at least the seventeenth century, with regional cuts: the Khevsur highland variant is richly embroidered in wool, while the plain dark chokha of the lowlands is the classic civic and military coat. After generations of everyday use the chokha is today reserved for festivals, folk dance, weddings and ceremonial occasions, and it remains the strongest single emblem of Georgian national dress.
source: Georgian National Museum, Tbilisi; ethnographic dress studies of the Caucasus

name: Kantsi (Georgian Drinking Horn)
description: The kantsi is the drinking horn of the Georgian highlands, cut from the curved horn of an ox, aurochs or mountain goat, polished, and often mounted at the rim in chased silver, sometimes with a small stand or a chain to hang it by. It is the fixed vessel of the supra, the Georgian feast, where the tamada raises the horn for each toast and custom requires it to be drained to the bottom in one draught before it is passed on; to drink from the kantsi is to honour the wine, the host and the speaker. The largest horns, holding a litre or more, are prized heirlooms of Svaneti and Khevsureti, and the same vessels appear in medieval Georgian manuscripts and in modern feast painting. Because the horn cannot be set down with wine in it, every toast must be finished, which is why the kantsi is remembered as the instrument of Georgian generosity.
material: ox or goat horn, chased silver (festive examples)
source: Russian Museum of Ethnography collections; Georgian feast (supra) custom studies

name: Panduri (Georgian Three-String Lute)
description: The panduri is the three-string fretted lute of eastern Georgia, a shallow wooden instrument carved from a single block of mulberry, walnut or other fruitwood, with a short neck, three strings and a soft, bright voice. It belongs to Kartli and Kakheti, where it accompanies men's table songs and the solo and choral polyphony of the region, the player strumming or plucking the strings to support the voice. Custom held that the panduri should hang on the wall of the house when not in use, ready for songs, and it was treated as a companion of family and village life rather than a mere concert instrument. With its larger four-string cousin the chonguri, the panduri is the most common plucked instrument of Georgian folk music and a familiar emblem of Georgian tradition, taught in music schools and played at every supra.
material: mulberry or other wood, gut/nylon strings
source: Georgian folk music tradition; hangebi.ge folk instrument documentation

name: Chonguri (Georgian Four-String Lute)
description: The chonguri is the four-string fretless lute of western Georgia, carved from a single block of walnut or maple into a shallow bowl, with a flat spruce soundboard and a short drone string called the zili that buzzes beneath the melody strings. It is the instrument of Guria and Samegrelo, where it traditionally accompanied women's songs and the nadi, the evening working gatherings at which women spun, wove and sang, and where the chonguri's quiet, flexible tone fitted a female voice. Unlike the fretted panduri of the east, the chonguri is played with a light, flowing touch, and its three melody strings are named after the three voices of Georgian polyphony. Still made and taught today, the chonguri belongs to the living polyphonic tradition that UNESCO inscribed in 2008.
material: walnut or maple, spruce soundboard, nylon strings
source: Smithsonian 'Georgian Chonguri' object of the day; Georgian folk instrument studies (Arakishvili)

name: Chuniri (Svan Bowed Fiddle)
description: The chuniri is the bowed fiddle of the Georgian mountain province of Svaneti, a round or tubular wooden body with a skin soundboard, three gut or horsehair strings and a heavy bow, held against the shoulder like a small violin. Because a bowed string can sustain a note, the chuniri is said to sing in place of a human voice, standing in for a singer in Svan hunting songs, work songs and choral polyphony; its two-string cousin, the chianuri, serves the same role in other highland regions such as Racha and Adjara. The instrument was the personal companion of Svan shepherds and hunters, who played it at home, at vigils and in the towers of the mountain villages. It remains one of the two bowed instruments of Georgia, heard at festivals and in the polyphonic ensembles that carry Svan tradition.
material: wood body, skin soundboard, horsehair strings
source: Wikipedia 'Chuniri'; Georgian folk music instrument documentation

name: Qvevri (Georgian Wine Vessel)
description: The qvevri is the great egg-shaped earthenware vessel of Georgia in which wine is fermented and aged, buried up to its neck in the floor of the marani, the wine cellar, so that only the clay rim and lid rise above the ground. Grape must, skins and stems all go into the qvevri and rest there for months, the cool earth holding a steady temperature, which gives amber wines their tannic, textured character and the method its special place in winemaking. Potters coil the vessels by hand from local clay, line them with beeswax and fire them without glaze; archaeological finds from the Shulaveri-Shomutepe culture date the method some 8,000 years, making qvevri wine among the oldest in the world. In 2013 UNESCO inscribed the ancient Georgian traditional qvevri wine-making method on the Representative List, and the buried qvevri remains the heart of Kakhetian cellar life.
source: UNESCO ICH 'Ancient Georgian traditional Qvevri wine-making method' (2013)

name: Khachkar (Armenian Cross-Stone)
description: The khachkar is the Armenian cross-stone, a freestanding stele carved from a single slab of local stone, most often the volcanic tuff of the Armenian plateau, its face dominated by an ornamented cross set over a rosette or a wheel of eternity. Around the cross the carver fills the stone with interlace, vine scrolls, leaves, pomegranates and birds, and the whole composition is framed in a decorated border; the earliest dated example bears the year 879, and the art reached its richest period from the thirteenth century. Khachkars were raised as tombstones, memorials for the dead, church dedications and thanksgivings, linking the everyday and the divine, the village and the monastery. In 2010 UNESCO inscribed the symbolism and craftsmanship of khachkars on the Representative List, and carved examples stand at Armenian churches from Julfa to Jerusalem.
material: volcanic tuff or other local stone
source: UNESCO ICH 'Armenian cross-stones art. Symbolism and craftsmanship of Khachkars' (2010)

name: Duduk (Armenian Double-Reed Flute)
description: The duduk is the double-reed woodwind of Armenia, carved from apricot wood into a short cylindrical tube fitted with a wide, flat reed, and played with circular breathing so the sound never stops. The technique of breathing in through the nose while squeezing air from the cheeks gives the duduk its characteristic long, breathy, singing notes, and the instrument is called the voice of Armenia for its warm, mournful tone. It accompanies folk songs, dances and round dances, but above all the lament, and it pairs with songs of mourning and love at weddings, funerals and the great feast days. In 2008 UNESCO inscribed duduk music on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and the instrument has also found a wider audience in world music and film scores.
source: UNESCO ICH 'Duduk and its music' (2008)

name: Tar (Azerbaijani Long-Necked Lute)
description: The Azerbaijani tar is a long-necked plucked lute with a deep figure-of-eight body, a lambskin soundboard and three courses of steel strings, played with a small plectrum held between the fingers. Master-builders hollow the body from mulberry wood, and the instrument's design was refined in the nineteenth century, when the tar became the leading solo and ensemble instrument of Azerbaijani music. It leads the mugham trio of tar, kamancha and frame drum that performs the classical modal suites of Azerbaijani tradition, and it accompanies ashiq narrative song as well. In 2012 UNESCO inscribed the craftsmanship and performance art of the tar on the Representative List, and Azerbaijani composers have written concert works for the instrument, making it a rare folk lute with a classical repertoire.
material: mulberry wood, lambskin soundboard, steel strings
source: UNESCO ICH 'Craftsmanship and performance art of the Tar' (2012)

name: Kamancha (Azerbaijani Spike Fiddle)
description: The kamancha is the bowed spike fiddle of Azerbaijan, built with a spherical or bowl-shaped wooden body covered with fish- or lambskin, a long neck that pierces the body, and four steel strings, played upright with the bow resting on the knee. Its bright, precise tone carries well indoors, which is why the kamancha sits beside the tar in the mugham trio and in the ensembles of Azerbaijani folk music, doubling and answering the melodic line. The instrument has a long history across the Caucasus, Persia and Central Asia under the name kamancheh, and Azerbaijani craftsmen and players developed their own distinguished school. In 2017 UNESCO inscribed the art of crafting and playing the kamancha on the Representative List, and the instrument remains central both to classical mugham and to the folk music of weddings and festivals.
material: walnut or mulberry wood, skin soundboard, steel strings
source: UNESCO ICH 'Art of crafting and playing with kamancha' (2017)

name: Kelaghayi (Azerbaijani Silk Headscarf)
description: The kelaghayi is the square silk headscarf of Azerbaijani women, woven on narrow silk looms in the town of Sheki and the village of Basgal, then dyed and printed with woodblocks so that a patterned border frames a plainer field. The classic ornament is the buta, the curved teardrop or flame motif that runs along the edge, and the colours carry meaning: white and light shades for older women and mourning, red and bright colours for brides and young women. The scarf is folded and tied in many ways - under the chin, at the back, or draped over the shoulders - and it belongs to daily wear, weddings, funerals and religious observance alike, its symbolism bound up with the woman's age and occasion. In 2014 UNESCO inscribed the traditional art and symbolism of the kelaghayi on the Representative List, and silk masters in Basgal still print the scarves by hand.
era: silk tradition from c. 7th century; kelaghayi to present
source: UNESCO ICH 'Traditional art and symbolism of Kelaghayi' (2014)

name: Shebeke (Sheki Stained-Glass Lattice)
description: Shebeke is the stained-glass lattice window of the Azerbaijani town of Sheki, built by fitting hundreds of small panes of coloured glass into a web of walnut strips that hold together by interlocking notches, without glue, nails or any backing frame. Each joint is cut and fitted by hand, and a single panel can take months of patient work, which is why the masters call the craft the art of patience. The finest surviving example is the Sheki Khan's Palace of 1762, whose roughly 190 windows hold up to five thousand glass fragments, throwing soft blue, red and green light across the painted walls of the palace. Since the palace was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019, the surviving shebeke workshops have revived the craft, training new masters in the old joinery.
source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Historic Centre of Sheki with the Khan's Palace' (2019); Art of Shebeke (national ICH inventory)

name: Shahmaran Amulet
description: The Shahmaran amulet carries the image of the serpent queen of Caucasian and Anatolian legend, a being with the head of a beautiful woman and the body of a serpent, who is said to have taught healing and the secrets of nature to those who dwelt in her underground kingdom. Silver and brass amulets, pendants, bracelets and wall plaques bearing her figure are worn or hung to turn away the evil eye and to bring luck and health, and her serpent-woman form appears on carpets, on jewellery and throughout the traditional story cycle of Azerbaijan, Turkey and Iran. The British Museum holds amulets of the serpent queen, and the legend of Shahmaran survives strongly in folk belief, especially among women who seek her protection in childbirth and sickness. As a wearable image of a living folk deity, the Shahmaran amulet links ancient serpent worship to modern jewellery.
material: silver or brass, engraved or painted serpent-queen image
source: British Museum collection (E AF.77); Shahmaran legend of Azerbaijan and Anatolia

name: Lahij Copperware
description: Lahij copperware is the hammered copper and brass craft of the mountain village of Lahij in Azerbaijan's Ismayilli district, where smiths have worked for centuries in a tight warren of craftsmen's streets. A vessel such as an ewer, basin, cauldron or tray is raised from a single sheet of metal by hammering, never cast or soldered, then engraved with geometric rosettes, floral scrolls and inscriptions, and finally coated with a silvery tin alloy that protects the copper. The craft flourished in the nineteenth century, when Lahij's copper goods travelled the Silk Road and were sold in Baku, Tbilisi and Persian cities, and the village's self-governing craft guilds kept the techniques alive. In 2015 UNESCO inscribed the copper craftsmanship of Lahij on the Representative List, and master coppersmiths still work in the old street, training apprentices in hammer, chisel and furnace.
source: UNESCO ICH 'Copper craftsmanship of Lahij' (2015)

name: Azerbaijani Carpet
description: The Azerbaijani carpet is the hand-knotted pile rug of Azerbaijan, woven on vertical looms in distinct regional schools - Karabakh, Shirvan, Tabriz, Baku, Gazakh and Ganja among them - each with its own palette, knot and field layout. The traditional repertoire of motifs includes the buta, the dragon, the medallion, the stylised garden and the khoncha offering tray, and the carpets combine rich reds, blues and ivories dyed from madder, indigo and walnut husk. Weaving was and is a women's craft, learned in the family, with the design passing from mother to daughter and the loom set up for dowry carpets that would serve the household for generations. In 2010 UNESCO inscribed the traditional art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving on the Representative List, and the carpet remains Azerbaijan's best-known craft, displayed in national museums and in the carpet museum of Baku.
material: wool pile, cotton warp, natural dyes
era: attested from the Middle Ages; classical schools 16th-19th century
source: UNESCO ICH 'Traditional art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving' (2010)
